title: 🚀 Mission to Mars
theme: Lead humanity's first crewed mission to Mars
description: You are the Mission Commander of Ares-1, humanity's first crewed mission to Mars. With a crew of 6, limited supplies, and 250 million kilometers of empty space between you and home, every decision could mean the difference between success and disaster. Manage resources, morale, and unexpected crises as you navigate the most ambitious journey in human history.

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: Read each mission scenario as Commander of the Ares-1 Mars mission
Choose how to respond — each option affects crew morale, resources, mission success, and more
Watch how your decisions affect Ship Systems, Crew Morale, and Mission Progress
Manage your limited Supply Points across 8 critical decision rounds
Complete the mission and bring your crew home safely
tips: Crew morale affects how well your team performs in emergencies
Conserving resources early gives you more options later
There's no perfect answer — real leadership means tough trade-offs

learning_objectives: Practice crisis decision-making under extreme resource constraints and time pressure
Develop team leadership skills including delegation, conflict resolution, and morale management
Understand the ethics of leadership when lives depend on your choices
Build strategic thinking by balancing short-term survival against long-term mission goals
Learn how scientific reasoning and risk assessment guide real-world decisions

player_profile.name: Mission Commander
player_profile.goal: Successfully complete humanity's first Mars mission
player_profile.background: Veteran astronaut and former Air Force pilot selected to lead the Ares-1 mission

coaching_moment: Knowing when to take a risk and when to play safe is one of the most important life skills.

rounds.title: Round 1: Crew Selection
rounds.story:
Launch is in 48 hours. A last-minute medical issue has grounded your planned geologist. You must choose a replacement from three candidates.

Current status:
• Supply Points: {{mento_coins}}
• Crew Morale: {{crew_morale}}%
• Ship Systems: {{ship_systems}}%

Candidate profiles:
• **Dr. Sarah Chen** — Brilliant geologist but has never been to space. Top academic credentials. Nervous but eager.
• **Major Tom Rivera** — Experienced astronaut, cross-trained in geology. Solid but not exceptional at either specialty.
• **Dr. Amir Patel** — Geologist with one prior space mission. Strong candidate but had a conflict with your flight engineer during training.

Who joins the crew?
rounds.goal: Select the right team member balancing competence, experience, and team dynamics

choices.label: Choose Dr. Sarah Chen
choices.description: The best geologist available. Her lack of space experience is a risk, but her expertise could make groundbreaking discoveries on Mars. Science is the mission's primary goal.
choices.feedback: Dr. Chen adapted quickly to zero-G, though the first week was rough. Her geological expertise proved invaluable — she identified mineral formations that changed the mission's scientific value. Sometimes betting on raw talent pays off.

choices.label: Choose Major Tom Rivera
choices.description: A safe, reliable choice. Won't be the best geologist, but his space experience means fewer risks. The jack-of-all-trades who won't let you down.
choices.feedback: Tom slotted in seamlessly. No drama, no surprises. His space experience kept the crew calm during early turbulence. Solid choice, though the science team wishes they had a stronger geologist for surface operations.

choices.label: Choose Dr. Amir Patel
choices.description: The complete package — space experience AND geology expertise. The personality conflict with your flight engineer is concerning, but professionals should be able to work together.
choices.feedback: Amir's skills were outstanding, but the tension with flight engineer Kowalski created an undercurrent of stress. Small conflicts in a tin can 250 million km from home have a way of growing. You'll need to manage this carefully.

rounds.coaching_moment: The best team isn't always the most talented individuals — it's the group that works best together.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What mattered most in your choice — skill, safety, or team chemistry? Why?

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: Round 2: The Rationing Decision
rounds.story:
Three months into the journey, a routine audit reveals a problem: a micro-meteorite damaged one of the water recycling units. You're losing 15% more water than planned.

You have enough to reach Mars, but margins are razor-thin. You need to cut consumption somewhere.

Current status:
• Supply Points: {{mento_coins}}
• Crew Health: {{crew_health}}%
• Crew Morale: {{crew_morale}}%
• Ship Systems: {{ship_systems}}%

Options involve trade-offs between comfort, health, science, and morale.

How do you manage the water crisis?
rounds.goal: Make resource allocation decisions with real consequences

choices.label: Equal Cuts for Everyone
choices.description: Reduce water rations by 20% across the board — including yourself. Everyone sacrifices equally. Fair but uncomfortable. Showers reduced, food options limited.
choices.feedback: The crew respected your fairness — you took the same cuts. But after two months of reduced rations, energy levels dropped and tempers shortened. Equal sacrifice builds solidarity, but prolonged deprivation takes a toll on everyone.

choices.label: Priority-Based Rationing
choices.description: Cut non-essential water use (longer showers, extra food prep) but protect drinking water and critical medical reserves. Some crew get more based on their physical roles — EVA team needs more hydration.
choices.feedback: Medically sound but socially complicated. The EVA team felt vindicated while others felt like second-class crew. Functional rationing makes sense on paper but creates hierarchy in a place where equality matters for survival.

choices.label: Attempt to Repair the Unit
choices.description: Divert engineering resources to fix the damaged recycling unit. High-risk: if it works, problem solved. If it fails, you've lost time and potentially made things worse.
choices.feedback: Your engineer spent 3 intense days on the repair. Success! The unit is back to 95% capacity. But it cost valuable supply materials and delayed several experiments. Sometimes the bold fix saves more than cautious conservation.

choices.label: Cut Science Experiments
choices.description: Many experiments use water. Pause non-critical research to preserve water for crew survival. Science can wait — lives can't.
choices.feedback: The crew stayed healthier, but the science team was devastated. Earth mission control questioned why you're going to Mars if not for science. Sometimes survival trumps the mission — but at what cost to purpose?

rounds.coaching_moment: Resource constraints force us to reveal our true priorities. What you protect when you can't protect everything shows what you really value.
rounds.reflection_prompt: When resources are scarce, do you optimize for fairness, efficiency, or creativity?

expert_pick.reason: Resilience research shows that processing setbacks openly builds stronger teams.

rounds.title: Round 3: The Solar Storm
rounds.story:
EMERGENCY ALERT: A massive solar storm is heading your way. You have 4 hours before it hits.

The radiation could be lethal if the crew is unprotected. Your options all have serious trade-offs.

Current status:
• Ship Systems: {{ship_systems}}%
• Crew Health: {{crew_health}}%
• Mission Progress: {{mission_progress}}%

Your radiation shelter can protect the crew, but it means shutting down most ship systems for 12-48 hours. Or you could try a risky maneuver to partially shield the ship using Mars's magnetic shadow — but that changes your trajectory.

Seconds count. What's your call, Commander?
rounds.goal: Make life-or-death decisions under extreme time pressure

choices.label: Full Radiation Shelter Protocol
choices.description: Everyone into the shielded compartment immediately. Shut down non-essential systems. Safe but you'll lose 2 days of mission time and some experiments will be ruined.
choices.feedback: The crew huddled in the shelter for 36 hours. Cramped, boring, but alive. Some experiments were lost, but everyone was safe. When lives are at stake, caution isn't cowardice — it's wisdom.

choices.label: Magnetic Shadow Maneuver
choices.description: Attempt to use Mars's magnetosphere for partial shielding. Requires precise navigation and burns extra fuel. If it works, minimal disruption. If miscalculated, the crew gets higher radiation exposure.
choices.feedback: The maneuver mostly worked — radiation exposure was reduced but not eliminated. Two crew members showed mild symptoms. A daring move that preserved mission timeline but at a health cost. Bold leaders must accept that bold moves have uncertain outcomes.

choices.label: Partial Shelter with Rotating Watches
choices.description: Keep essential systems running with rotating 2-person watches outside the shelter. Everyone gets some exposure, but the ship stays operational. Share the risk.
choices.feedback: The rotating watch system worked, though everyone received low-level radiation. The crew bonded over shared sacrifice — nobody was asked to take more risk than anyone else. Shared hardship builds unbreakable teams.

rounds.coaching_moment: In a crisis, the best decision is often the one you can make quickly and commit to fully. Hesitation can be more dangerous than an imperfect choice.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Under pressure, did you prioritize safety, mission, or team unity? What does that say about your leadership instinct?

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Round 4: Crew Tensions
rounds.story:
Six months in space. The novelty is gone. Tempers are rising.

Dr. Kowalski (flight engineer) and Dr. Lopez (biologist) had a heated argument that turned personal. Kowalski called Lopez's experiments "a waste of resources." Lopez called Kowalski "a wrench-turner who doesn't understand science."

Now they refuse to work in the same module. In a ship this small, that's not sustainable.

Current status:
• Team Cohesion: {{team_cohesion}}%
• Crew Morale: {{crew_morale}}%
• Crew Health: {{crew_health}}%

Other crew members are taking sides. The tension is affecting everyone's sleep and performance.

How do you handle this, Commander?
rounds.goal: Resolve interpersonal conflict in a high-stress, isolated environment

choices.label: Formal Mediation Session
choices.description: Sit both down for a structured mediation. Each person gets uninterrupted time to speak. Identify the root cause. Establish ground rules for coexistence. This isn't optional — it's an order.
choices.feedback: The mediation revealed that Kowalski felt undervalued (engineers 'just fix things') while Lopez felt her science was dismissed. Once each heard the other's frustration, defensiveness melted. They're not best friends, but they're professional. Sometimes people just need to be heard.

choices.label: Restructure Work Schedules
choices.description: Rearrange shifts so they rarely overlap. Give each their own space and responsibilities. Minimize contact. They don't have to like each other — they just have to not interfere with each other.
choices.feedback: The avoidance strategy reduced visible conflict but created operational inefficiencies. Cross-team coordination suffered. On a 6-person crew, you can't afford silos. Avoiding problems doesn't make them disappear — it just makes them quieter.

choices.label: Assign Them a Joint Mission
choices.description: Give Kowalski and Lopez a critical task that requires both their skills — calibrating the bio-engineering module for Mars surface prep. They'll have to work together or the mission suffers.
choices.feedback: Forced collaboration was tense at first. But when they solved a tricky calibration problem together, something shifted. Shared accomplishment built mutual respect that words never could. Sometimes you have to push people toward growth, not comfort.

choices.label: Command Decision: Enforce Professionalism
choices.description: Lay down the law. On this ship, personal conflicts don't exist. They will be professional or face formal disciplinary notes that follow them home. Military discipline keeps ships running.
choices.feedback: They complied. But compliance without resolution breeds resentment. The crew saw you as harsh rather than fair. Fear keeps order temporarily — but on an 18-month mission, fear corrodes trust. Authority works best when paired with empathy.

rounds.coaching_moment: In any team, conflict is inevitable. How you handle it — ignore, suppress, or transform — determines your team's ultimate strength.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Do you tend to avoid conflict, confront it, or try to transform it? Which approach builds lasting trust?

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Round 5: The Signal
rounds.story:
Your communications officer picks up something extraordinary: a repeating, structured radio signal emanating from the Martian surface. It doesn't match any known natural phenomenon or equipment signature.

The signal is patterned — almost like a sequence. Mathematically structured.

Current status:
• Scientific Data: {{scientific_data}}%
• Earth Trust: {{earth_trust}}%
• Crew Morale: {{crew_morale}}%

Earth mission control says: 'Investigate but proceed with extreme caution.' The crew is split between excitement and fear.

This could be the greatest discovery in human history — or a natural anomaly. How do you proceed?
rounds.goal: Navigate uncertainty and make decisions when the stakes are unknowable

choices.label: Systematic Scientific Investigation
choices.description: Run every possible analysis before drawing conclusions. Cross-reference with all known natural signals. Document everything meticulously. Don't jump to conclusions — let the data speak.
choices.feedback: Weeks of careful analysis revealed the signal was likely geological — subsurface ice formations creating harmonic resonances. Not alien life, but a fascinating natural phenomenon worth studying. The scientific method isn't exciting, but it's reliable. Truth doesn't care about our hopes.

choices.label: Redirect Mission to Signal Source
choices.description: This could be the most important discovery ever. Redirect landing site to the signal origin. If there's even a 1% chance this is extraterrestrial, it's worth investigating immediately.
choices.feedback: The detour consumed extra fuel and complicated the landing plan. The signal source turned out to be a natural geological formation — impressive but not alien. Your enthusiasm cost the mission resources. Excitement is not a strategy.

choices.label: Let Earth Mission Control Decide
choices.description: This is too big for one person. Send all data to Earth and let the world's best scientists and policymakers determine next steps. Follow the chain of command.
choices.feedback: Earth took 3 weeks to deliberate (plus signal delay). By then the window for optimal investigation had passed. The crew felt sidelined from the biggest moment of the mission. Sometimes waiting for consensus means missing the moment.

rounds.coaching_moment: When facing the unknown, the most important tool is not technology — it's the discipline to question your own assumptions.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How do you handle uncertainty — with excitement, caution, or by deferring to others? What drives that instinct?

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: Round 6: Mars Landing
rounds.story:
The moment has arrived. Mars fills the viewport. But the landing computer flags a problem: your primary landing zone has unexpected dust storm activity. Visibility is near zero.

Current status:
• Ship Systems: {{ship_systems}}%
• Mission Progress: {{mission_progress}}%
• Crew Health: {{crew_health}}%
• Crew Morale: {{crew_morale}}%

You have three options, and you need to decide in the next 20 minutes before orbital mechanics take the choice away from you.

The crew is suited up and ready. Everyone is silent, watching you.
rounds.goal: Make a critical go/no-go decision with incomplete information

choices.label: Divert to Backup Landing Zone
choices.description: Switch to the secondary landing site 200km north. Clear weather but less scientifically interesting. The safer choice — you'll still be on Mars, just not where you planned.
choices.feedback: Textbook landing at the backup site. The crew cheered as boots touched Martian soil. The secondary site turned out to have its own scientific treasures. Flexibility saved the mission. Perfection is the enemy of good enough.

choices.label: Wait in Orbit for Storm to Clear
choices.description: Stay in orbit for 48-72 hours until the dust storm passes. Costs fuel and time, but you'll land at the planned site with full visibility. Patience over impulse.
choices.feedback: The storm cleared in 60 hours. Landing at the primary site was perfect. But the orbital wait consumed fuel reserves that would have been useful later. Patience is a virtue, but it has a price tag. Every delay in space costs resources.

choices.label: Land Through the Storm
choices.description: Trust the instruments and your pilot. Attempt landing at the primary site despite reduced visibility. High risk, but landing computers can handle most of it. This is what you trained for.
choices.feedback: A harrowing descent. The ship took minor damage on landing and one crew member was injured by turbulence. But you're on Mars at the primary site. The crew is shaken but proud. Bold choices have both costs and rewards — leadership means accepting both.

rounds.coaching_moment: The best decision is often not the perfect one — it's the one you can execute well with the information you have.
rounds.reflection_prompt: When you face a high-stakes decision with incomplete information, do you tend to play safe, wait for clarity, or push forward?

expert_pick.reason: The most effective leaders adapt their approach based on the situation — not habit.

rounds.title: Round 7: The Discovery
rounds.story:
On the Martian surface, your geology team makes an extraordinary find: microbial fossils in a rock formation. Evidence of ancient Martian life.

The scientific community will go wild — but there's a complication. The fossils are located in an unstable cave system. Extracting proper samples requires sending a team deep inside, which your safety officer says is dangerously risky.

Current status:
• Scientific Data: {{scientific_data}}%
• Crew Health: {{crew_health}}%
• Earth Trust: {{earth_trust}}%
• Supply Points: {{mento_coins}}

The science team wants to go in. The safety officer says absolutely not. Earth is urging "maximum scientific return."

Your call, Commander.
rounds.goal: Balance scientific ambition against crew safety

choices.label: Send Full Team Into the Cave
choices.description: This is why we came to Mars. Send 3 crew members with full equipment for a thorough 6-hour expedition. The risk is real but the discovery could change human understanding forever.
choices.feedback: The team extracted pristine samples — proof of ancient Martian microbial life. But a partial cave collapse injured one team member (non-critical). Earth celebrated the discovery while debating whether you risked too much. History will judge whether the reward justified the risk.

choices.label: Send Robotic Probe Only
choices.description: Deploy the rover and remote sampling arm into the cave. Slower, less thorough, but zero risk to crew. If the robots find something extraordinary, reassess sending humans.
choices.feedback: The rover retrieved partial samples — enough to confirm microbial fossils but not enough for comprehensive analysis. The science team was frustrated but alive and healthy. You preserved your most valuable resource: your crew. Sometimes 'good enough' science beats perfect science at too high a cost.

choices.label: Quick 2-Person Survey
choices.description: Send 2 crew members for a rapid 90-minute survey and grab-samples. Quick in, quick out. Limited science but human eyes on the discovery. Compromise between ambition and safety.
choices.feedback: The quick survey gathered critical samples and visual documentation. No injuries. The science team wished for more time but understood. You found the middle ground between caution and ambition. Not every decision needs to be all-or-nothing.

rounds.coaching_moment: When the potential reward is enormous, the temptation to take excessive risk grows. Great leaders resist that temptation without killing ambition entirely.
rounds.reflection_prompt: If your choice had led to someone getting seriously hurt, would you still feel it was the right call? How do you evaluate decisions — by outcomes or by the reasoning behind them?

expert_pick.reason: Calculated risk-taking is what separates growth-oriented leaders from status-quo managers.

rounds.title: Round 8: The Long Road Home
rounds.story:
Mission objectives complete. Time to go home. But there's one final challenge.

During pre-departure checks, you discover the main engine has micro-fractures from the landing impact. Your engineer says it will probably hold for the return trip — 85% confidence. But 'probably' means 15% chance of catastrophic failure.

You can attempt repairs, which will delay departure by 2 weeks and consume most remaining supplies. Or you can launch on schedule and hope the engine holds.

Current status:
• Ship Systems: {{ship_systems}}%
• Crew Health: {{crew_health}}%
• Supply Points: {{mento_coins}}
• Crew Morale: {{crew_morale}}%

The crew is exhausted and wants to go home. Staying longer on Mars means more rationing and more time away from families. But leaving with a damaged engine...

Final decision, Commander. How do you bring your crew home?
rounds.goal: Make the final leadership decision that determines the mission's legacy

choices.label: Repair Before Departure
choices.description: Stay 2 extra weeks. Repair the engine properly. Leave with confidence. The crew won't like the delay, but everyone goes home safely. No unnecessary risks on the return trip.
choices.feedback: Two hard weeks of repairs and strict rationing. The crew was miserable but the engine was solid. The return journey was smooth and safe. You arrived home 2 weeks late but with everyone alive. Earth celebrated not just the science, but the leadership that prioritized lives over schedules.

choices.label: Launch on Schedule
choices.description: 85% is good odds. The crew needs to go home. Every extra day on Mars drains supplies and morale. The engine has redundant systems — it will hold. Trust the engineering.
choices.feedback: Launch day. The engine held — barely. Warning lights flickered during the Mars departure burn but stabilized. The return journey had tense moments, but you made it home on time. Sometimes luck favors the bold, but counting on luck isn't leadership — it's gambling.

choices.label: Quick Patch and Launch in 5 Days
choices.description: Do the most critical repairs in 5 days — reinforce the worst fractures, test under controlled burns. Not perfect, but brings confidence from 85% to roughly 95%. Compromise between speed and safety.
choices.feedback: The partial repair was smart. Five focused days of work addressed the critical fractures. The return journey was smooth with no engine issues. You found the sweet spot between thoroughness and pragmatism. Not every problem needs a perfect solution — sometimes 'good enough, done fast' is the best answer.

choices.label: Request Earth Rescue Mission
choices.description: Report the engine issue and request a rescue ship. It will take months, but it's the safest option. Your crew's lives are not worth gambling on 85% odds.
choices.feedback: The rescue ship took 8 additional months. Your crew survived but the extended stay broke morale and strained resources to the limit. Earth questioned whether the caution was justified. Being too cautious can be as costly as being too bold. Leadership is finding the balance.

rounds.coaching_moment: The final decision of any mission reveals the leader you've become. Every choice you've made has led to this moment.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Looking back at all your decisions across this mission, what pattern do you see? Are you proud of the commander you've been?

expert_pick.reason: Research shows that patience-based decisions lead to 3x better long-term outcomes.

achievements.title: Crew Keeper
achievements.description: Maintain crew health above 70% throughout the mission

endings.title: Legendary Commander
endings.description: You brought the crew home safely with outstanding scientific results. History will remember you as one of the greatest space commanders.

endings.title: Safe Return
endings.description: Everyone came home healthy. The mission results were mixed, but no one can question your commitment to your crew.

endings.title: Science Pioneer
endings.description: The scientific data you collected will advance human knowledge for decades. But the cost to your crew was significant.

endings.title: Hard Lessons
endings.description: The mission had challenges, and not every decision worked out. But you learned what it means to lead — and that's a discovery worth more than any Mars sample.

glossary_terms.definition: The leader responsible for all decisions and crew safety during a space mission
Extra-Vehicular Activity — any activity done by an astronaut outside the spacecraft
A heavily shielded area of the spacecraft designed to protect crew from solar radiation
The physics of how objects move in space, which determines launch windows and trajectories
The region around a planet dominated by its magnetic field, which can deflect solar radiation
A tiny space rock that can cause damage to spacecraft at high velocities
A risk taken after careful analysis of potential outcomes and probabilities

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 1: 🚀 Mission to Mars Basics

questions.question: What is 'empathy'?
questions.explanation: Empathy is the ability to understand and share the feelings of others.

questions.question: A good leader should:

choices.text: Listen to the team and consider different views

questions.explanation: Good leaders listen to diverse perspectives before making informed decisions.

questions.question: What does 'delayed gratification' mean?

choices.text: Waiting for a bigger reward instead of taking a smaller one now

questions.explanation: Delayed gratification means resisting a smaller immediate reward for a larger future one.
